video.title: THIS ONE SIN Keeps Many Souls in PURGATORY — And They Never Confessed It || Blessed Fulton Sheen
video.description:
What sin is so often overlooked, hidden, or left unconfessed? And what can the reality of Purgatory teach us about the importance of repentance and preparing our souls for eternity?

In this powerful 41-minute message, Venerable Fulton J. Sheen shares timeless spiritual wisdom about Purgatory, sin, confession, repentance, God's mercy, judgment, and eternal life.

This message invites us to examine our conscience honestly and consider whether there are sins, attachments, or habits we have failed to bring before God with sincere repentance.

WHAT YOU WILL DISCOVER:

• The sin and spiritual danger explored in this message
• Why some sins can remain hidden from others
• The importance of sincere confession and repentance
• What Purgatory teaches us about purification and eternity
• Why examining your conscience matters
• How God's mercy calls us toward conversion
• Timeless reflections associated with Venerable Fulton J. Sheen

Purgatory reminds us of the seriousness of sin and the need for holiness. Rather than waiting until the end of life, we are called to seek God's mercy, repent sincerely, and grow closer to Him today.

🙏 Take a moment to examine your conscience and pray for the Holy Souls in Purgatory.

If this message speaks to your heart, share it with someone who may need this spiritual reminder.

🔔 Subscribe to THE HIDDEN GOSPEL for timeless Catholic teachings, spiritual reflections, prayer, faith, repentance, and inspiring messages associated with Venerable Fulton J. Sheen.

THE HIDDEN GOSPEL — Discover timeless truths that can transform the soul.

transcript.text: Umberto Ferante traveled from Barleta to San Giovanni Rotondo to see Padre Pio.
Father Umberto was 31 years old, ordained for six years, and he was in trouble.
Not moral trouble, not doctrinal trouble, pastoral trouble.
He had a parish of 800 souls and he could not figure out why his church was dying.
The numbers were fine. Mass attendance was strong, the pews were full on Sundays.
The collection basket was adequate. The parish school had a waiting list.
By every measurable standard, St. Aine's in Barla was a thriving parish.
But Father Umberto could feel something beneath the numbers that the numbers could not capture.
A flatness, a greyness, a quality in the air of his church on Sunday mornings that was closer to a dentist's waiting room than to the house of God.
People came, people sat, people performed the liturgy with the precision of a well-rehearsed play, and then people left.

And in all of it, in the coming and the sitting, and the standing, and the kneeling, and the receiving, and the leaving, there was no life, no spark, no moment where Father Umberto could look out from the altar and see a single face that was moved by what was happening on the altar.
Not one face in 800.
He had tried everything.
New homily techniques, parish retreats, prayer groups, a youth program, a women's auxiliary, a men's sodality, more candles, better music, different hymns.
Nothing worked.
The people came, did what they had always done, and left feeling exactly the way they had always felt, which was nothing.
Father Umberto was not a man who gave up easily.
He had grown up in a farming family outside Barla, the third of six children, and he had the farmer's stubborn patience with things that grow slowly.
But this was not growing slowly, this was not growing at all.
It was standing still.

And he had begun to wonder whether the problem was him, whether he was failing his people in some way he could not identify, whether there was a deficiency in his priesthood that was poisoning the well of his parish and rendering everything he did spiritually inert.
So he went to Padre Pio, not for confession, though he made one for counsel.
He wanted to sit before a man who could see the spiritual world and ask him, what am I doing wrong?
He waited in line for seven hours.
When he finally knelt in the confessional, he made his confession first.

The usual sins of a young priest: impatience with an elderly parishioner who told the same story every Sunday, pride in a homily that had been well received, distraction during the liturgy of the hours, small things.
Padre Pio gave him absolution and then said, that is not why you came.
Father Umberto said, no Father, I came because my parish is dying and I do not know how to save it.
Padre Pio was quiet for a moment, then he said, your parish is not dying, it is asleep and there is a difference.
A dead thing cannot be revived, a sleeping thing only needs to be awakened.
Father Umberto felt a flicker of hope.
How do I wake them? He asked.
Padre Pio said, you cannot wake them until you understand what put them to sleep.
And what put them to sleep is the same thing that puts most Catholic parishes to sleep, the same thing that fills purgatory with more souls than any other sin: the sin of tepidity.
Hold on, because what Padre Pio explained next about tepidity is something I have searched for in catechisms and theology books for years and I have never found it stated so clearly anywhere else.
This is knowledge that came from direct spiritual vision, not from academic study, and it changes the way you understand your own faith.

Padre Pio said to Father Umberto, most people think that purgatory is filled with great sinners who barely repented in time, people who committed terrible acts and squeaked through the gates of mercy by a hair's breadth.
This is wrong.
The great sinners make up a very small percentage of purgatory.

transcript.text: while the slow patient fire of God's purifying love tries to kindle something in a soul that spent 70 or 80 years learning how to feel nothing.
Father Umberto said, but tidity is not a mortal sin.
How can it lead to purgatory?
Padre Pio said, it is not classified as a mortal sin by the theologians, but I have seen it with my own eyes, and I can tell you this.
Tupidity is the only sin that gets worse every time you receive the sacraments without being cured of it.
Every communion received in a state of tidity deepens the tidity.
Every confession made without acknowledging the tidity reinforces it.
Every mass attended without a single moment of genuine presence thickens the walls of the lukewarm prison.
Other sins weaken when you go to church.
This sin strengthens.

Father Umberto felt the blood leave his face because he understood suddenly that every program he had run, every retreat he had organized, every innovation he had introduced had been aimed at the symptoms rather than the disease.
He'd been trying to make his parish more active, more engaged, more organized, when what he should have been trying to do was make them more alive.
Padre Pio then did something that Father Umberto had not expected.
He began to describe specific souls he had seen in purgatory, not in general terms, in specific heartbreaking detail.

He said, I will tell you about three souls I have seen, three Catholics who lived lives that looked exactly like the lives of your parishioners, and all three are in purgatory for the sin of tidity, and all three are confused.
The first Padre Pio said was a man named Agostino, a pharmacist 61 years old when he died from a town not far from here.
He went to mass every Sunday of his adult life, 43 years of Sundays, more than 2,000 masses.
And in all of those masses, he never once wept at the consecration, not once.
He watched the priest raise the host, and he thought about his inventory.
He watched the chalice elevated, and he calculated the week's earnings.
He received the body of Christ on his tongue and felt less than he felt when he tasted his morning coffee.
2,000 opportunities to encounter the living God in the most intimate way possible.
2,000 times God came to him in the Eucharist, and 2,000 times Augustinino's heart was elsewhere.
Not in sin, not in rebellion, just elsewhere in the grey familiar comfortable elsewhere.
Elsewhere of a mind that had learned to be present in body and absent in soul.
Agostino never confessed this, not once in 43 years, because no priest ever told him it was a sin.
Because no homily he ever heard addressed the fact that receiving communion without interior presence is not merely a missed opportunity.
It is an offense, not an offense of malice, an offense of indifference.
And indifference to the presence of God is in the economy of the spiritual world more grievous than many sins of passion.
Because a sin of passion at least acknowledges that God's laws are real and worth breaking.

transcript.text: That is what my rosary had become, a commute, a daily trip from the first Hail Mary to the last Glory Be, be traveled with the same mechanical efficiency and the same spiritual absence as the drive from my house in Coventry to the Tesco on Warwick road.
I could do it with my eyes closed and that was the problem.
My eyes were closed, my heart was closed, the only thing open was my mouth, and mouths alone do not pray.
The third soul Padre Pio described to Father Umberto was the one that disturbed the young priest the most, because it was not an old person who had spent decades in tidity.
It was a young man, perhaps 22, Padre Pio said, an altar boy.
He had served at the altar since he was 12 years old, 10 years, 10 years of standing closer to the Eucharist than anyone else in the church except the priest.

10 years of holding the cruets, ringing the bells at the consecration, carrying the candles in procession, kneeling at the foot of the altar, while the body and blood of Christ were made present three feet from his face.
And in 10 years, he never once felt the presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
Not once he felt the weight of the cruits, he felt the heat of the candles.
He felt the cold of the marble floor through the knees of his cassock.
He felt everything except the one thing that the entire mass existed to make present, Christ, the living Christ standing three feet away.

And this young man's soul was so tepid, so accustomed to proximity without presence, that the most powerful encounter available to a human being, the encounter with God in the flesh, produced in him less sensation than a breeze through an open window.
Padre Pio said, this young man died in an accident, a fall from a scaffolding at a construction site.
He was 22, and when he arrived before God, he did not understand why he was being sent to purgatory.
He said, but I served at the altar, I was there every Sunday, I was closer to you than anyone.
And God said, you were close to my body, but you were far from my heart.
You stood in my presence the way a guard stands at a door, present in position, absent in devotion.
And the distance between your body and your soul during all those years at my altar is the distance you must now cross in purgatory.
Father Umberto was shaking.
He said, Father, how many of my parishioners are in this state?
Padre Pio said, I cannot tell you the number, but I can tell you this.
If you walked into your church on any given Sunday and could see what I see, the spiritual state of every soul in every pew, you would weep because the majority of them are tepid.
Not all, there are always a few souls in every parish who burn, a few whose prayers rise like incense, a few whose presence at Mass is a genuine encounter with the living God.

But the majority, Father, the vast comfortable majority are at room temperature, and they do not know it, and no one tells them, and they go home and come back next Sunday, and the temperature stays the same, and the years pass and the tidity hardens, and eventually they die.
And then they no hold on because there is a document that confirms everything Padre Pio said about tidity, and it is not a private revelation.
It is not a legend, it is in the Book of Revelation itself, and it is the most terrifying sentence Christ ever spoke.
In the third chapter of the Book of Revelation verse 16, Christ says to the church in Laodicea.

transcript.text: Correspondence pio that the Vatican examined during the canonization process.
It is not hearsay it is not legend.
It is Padre Pio in his own handwriting, in his own words, confirming that he saw stupidity as the most dangerous spiritual state a Catholic can inhabit.
More dangerous than active sin because active sin has an antidote.
It is called confession.
But tepidity has no antidote in the standard sacramental toolkit, because the tepid person does not know they are sick.
They go to confession and confess impatience and gossip and missing morning prayers.
They never confess the thing that is actually killing them.
I am lukewarm, I do not feel God's presence, my faith has no fire.
These words are never spoken in the confessional because the tepid person does not recognize them as a confession.
They recognize them if they recognize them at all, as a feeling, a mood, a phase, something that will pass, something that everyone goes through.
Not a sin, never a sin.
And this is where the hidden proof becomes devastating, because Padre Pio did not merely observe stupidity.
He tracked it.
He told Father Alberto that he had noticed a pattern among the tepid souls he had encountered over 50 years.
The pattern was this, tepidity is progressive.
It does not stay at the same temperature.
It cools slowly, imperceptibly, but relentlessly.
A soul that is lukewarm at 30 is cooler at 40, cooler still at 50.
By 60 it is approaching a spiritual coldness that is almost indistinguishable from the coldness of unbelief.
Not because the person has stopped believing, but because their belief has been drained of every last calorie of warmth.
Padre Pio described four stages of tidiness that he had observed.
He called them the four degrees of cooling.
The first degree is distraction.
This is where it begins, the soul is present at mass, but the mind is elsewhere.
The rosary is prayed, but the heart is not engaged.
Prayer becomes a task to be completed rather than an encounter to be experienced.
Most Catholics enter this stage at some point in their lives.
It is normal, it is not yet dangerous, but if it is not addressed, it deepens.
The second degree is routine.
The distraction becomes habitual.
The soul no longer even tries to be present during prayer.
It has accepted that prayer is a mechanical activity like brushing teeth, something done because it should be done, not because it produces anything.
The person still goes to mass, still prays, still receives the sacraments.
But the interior life has become as flat and featureless as a parking lot.
There is no landscape, no hills, no valleys, no beauty, just asphalt, just the same gray surface stretching in every direction.
The third degree is indifference.
The routine has calcified into a kind of spiritual numbness.
The person no longer notices that they are numb.
They no longer miss the fire because they have forgotten what fire feels like.
They hear the words of the gospel and they do not stir.
They receive communion and they do not tremble.
They see a crucifix and they do not weep, not because they are hardhearted, because they have become spiritually anesthetized.
The sacraments are still being administered, but they are being administered to a patient who cannot feel them.
The medicine is being poured into a vessel that has no bottom.
The fourth degree, Padre Pio said, and his voice dropped to a whisper when he said it, is comfort.
This is the final and most lethal stage.
The person has become so thoroughly tepid that they are comfortable in their tepidity.
They have built a life around it.
They have friends who are tepid, they attend a parish that is tepid, they read spiritual books that are tepid.
Everything in their world confirms that their temperature is normal and they are content.
This is the stage that Padre Pio said was almost impossible to reverse without a crisis, because the soul has sealed itself inside a comfortable room with no windows.
It cannot see the fire outside, it cannot feel the heat, it cannot smell the smoke, it is perfectly insulated and it is dying.
